EICMA 2026 • Here Are Some of the Serious and Obscure Brands That EICMA 2026 Had To Offer – Worth Knowing About
Jay Leno Drives a Backhoe Around LA, It Has an Engine That Hit 406 MPH
15 photos
Photo: Jay Leno's Garage | YouTube
Jay Leno started out in LA behind the wheel of a JCB 3CX Hydrogen backhoe loader, the world's first commercially available hydrogen combustion vehicle of its kind. The zero-tailpipe-emission construction machine is powered by the same engine architecture that set the mind-blowing 406.320 mph world land speed record.
No, Jay Leno isn't roaming the streets of Los Angeles at 400 mph (643.738 kph) because the JCB backhoe he has taken for a spin will by no means come anywhere near that speed. So he is moving around in a 19,180-pound (8,700-kilogram) monster.
The vehicle takes up an entire lane, measuring 18 feet 5 inches (5.62 meters) from the front loader bucket to the folded rear digging arm, 7 feet 9 inches (2.35 meters) across the rear tires, and 11 feet 10 inches (3.61 meters) to the top of the folded rear boom when driving on the road.
Jay Leno is sitting in a one-seat cab with a roof that stands at roughly 10 feet (3.0 meters), plus the protective cap housing the three hydrogen cylinders. The twist is that JCB planted the modified versions of its exact digger engine into a custom streamliner, designed entirely by computer and with zero wind tunnel testing.
Photo: Jay Leno's Garage | YouTube To transform an industrial construction engine into a powerplant capable of crossing the 400 mph barrier, JCB and Ricardo hand-built six race engines. While the engineers retained the crankshaft and basic block geometry, they came up with custom forged pistons, upgraded connecting rods, and a dry-sump lubrication system, specifically designed to keep oil flowing while the engine lies flat on its side.
On August 11, 2026, retired Royal Air Force pilot Andy Green drove the JCB Hydromax streamliner at the Bonneville Salt Flats in Utah. He achieved an FIA-confirmed two-way average of 406.320 mph (653.909 kph), after averaging 400.623 mph (644.740 kph) on the first run and 412.135 mph (663.267 kph) on the return. He smashed the previous combustion record of 185.5 mph (298.533 kph).
The 32-foot-long Hydromax was built by motorsport engineering firm Prodrive and powered by two production-based 4.8-liter JCB hydrogen internal combustion engines, adapted from JCB’s digger power plants.
While the commercial backhoe engine makes just 74 horsepower (75 metric horsepower) and 324 pound-feet (440 Newton meters) of torque, the engineering firm Ricardo upgraded the twin turbocharged engines to push out 800 horsepower and 1,300 pound-feet of torque each. That would be a combined 1,600 horsepower and 2,600 pound-feet of torque.
Photo: Jay Leno's Garage | YouTube Simple mathematics shows that each engine delivers more than ten times the power and roughly four times the torque of the 74-horsepower production JCB 448 ABH2 backhoe engine on which it is based.
Rather than generating electricity like a fuel cell, JCB's engine burns hydrogen gas in a traditional piston-and-cylinder setup, emitting only water vapor and zero carbon dioxide. Approved for commercial sale in Europe in early 2025, the JCB 3CX Hydrogen delivers the exact same digging power, torque, and rapid refueling times as a conventional diesel backhoe.
To handle that massive torque at over 400 mph, the Hydromax actually used standard clutches pulled straight from a production JCB backhoe loader like the one that Jay Leno took for a spin in the City of the Angels.
The engine that powers it is the same one that powered the world’s fastest hydrogen car to 406 mph. Not similar! The same! Ryan Ballard, Engineering Director at JCB, who led the engineering team for the JCB Hydromax, tells the story of the backhoe and of the vehicle that broke the speed record .
Photo: Jay Leno's Garage | YouTube He brought along Wing Commander Andy Green OBE, a retired British Royal Air Force fighter pilot and the only person in history to break the sound barrier on land. He hit a mind-blowing 763.035 mph (Mach 1.016) in 1997, and his record still stands today.
However, from inside the car, he never heard the thunder-like explosion created by an object travels through the air faster than the speed of sound. " Technically, I am the only person on the planet who never had the chance to hear the sonic boom, " Andy Green says.
Parked in Jay Leno's garage is the 32-foot, twin-engined hydrogen-powered land speed record streamliner built by JCB and driven by Andy Green. Sitting right next to it, carrying the same engine but looking worlds apart, is the JCB 3CX backhoe.
The model launched back in May 2026 to replace the traditional diesel engine with a zero-carbon hydrogen internal combustion engine, delivering the exact same digging, loading, and roading performance.
Photo: Jay Leno's Garage | YouTube The massive, bright yellow vehicle that Leno took for a spin in Los Angeles stores hydrogen at 350 bar of pressure in three carbon-fiber-wrapped aluminum tanks, sitting inside a protective cap on the cab roof. Regulators step that pressure down to under 20 bar before feeding the engine.
Filling the tanks from a ground-level port takes roughly ten minutes. A full tank of hydrogen provides approximately six hours of continuous operation. While the backhoe is ready to work, the JCB Hydromax's racing days are over. So it will most likely find a place in a museum once it completes its U.S. tour.

Gearhead Got 1970 Mustang Mach 1 in 1984, Raced It, Parked It 35 Years Ago, Never Touched It Since
48 photos
Photo: YouTube/Stay Tuned
“Presently stored in car trailer and does not run.. It is in need of restoration. Owned since the 1980s. I would rather see an enthusiast bring it back to life than have it continue sitting.” When a gearhead reads these words, the matter is pretty much settled. But when said gearhead is tagged by friends in a comment on the Facebook Marketplace ad for the car, it’s no longer simply car enthusiasm. It’s a mission.
Automotive builder and “Stay Tuned” YouTube channel host Tony Angelo recently abandoned his weekly shop schedule after viewers tagged him in an online listing for a genuine 1970 Ford Mustang Mach 1. Parked for the better part of 35 years, the fastback carries a 351-cubic-inch Cleveland V8 with a 4-speed manual transmission, a Traction-Lok rear axle, factory air conditioning, power steering, and power front disc brakes in a sought-after package.
Located in the Philadelphia area, the Mustang belonged to longtime owner Jeff Miller, who purchased it in 1984 and street-raced it along Front Street before storing it away in the late 1980s or early 1990s. Although the car wore an aging brown repaint over its original gold finish and carried a $16,500 asking price, Angelo arrived the next day with some old photos of dead US presidents, and negotiated. They shook hands at $15,000 for the project.
Considering that restored 1970 Mach 1 models routinely command between $60,000 and $75,000, Angelo viewed the purchase as a compelling bargain despite obvious cosmetic and mechanical neglect. Closer inspection revealed a rusted passenger door skin, a cracked windshield, and localized floor pan corrosion.
Photo: Facebook Marketplace/Jeff Miller The good news: the structural frame rails, pinch welds, and torque boxes remained remarkably intact, giving the Stay Tuned crew a solid foundation rather than the proverbial basket to carry hopes and prayers.
Back at the shop, Angelo and his team washed away decades of mold and grime before consulting automotive journalist David Freiburger regarding the engine's potential. Jeff had rebuilt the 351 Cleveland prior to parking the car, installing higher-compression TRW pistons, a hot Crane hydraulic camshaft, long-tube headers, and an Accel dual-point mechanical distributor, upgrading the V8 from its factory 300 horsepower rating toward an estimated 400 horsepower on the street.
Reviving an engine dormant for 35 years requires methodical preparation before the first turn of the key. The wrenchers verified that the crankshaft rotated freely, examined the clean cylinder walls and bottom-end bearings with a borescope, and poured equal parts acetone and automatic transmission fluid into each cylinder to free any stuck piston rings before draining the dry oil pan and fabricating a custom drain plug.
Photo: YouTube/Stay Tuned Because roughly 80 percent of internal engine wear occurs during dry startups, Angelo removed the distributor and spun the oil pump shaft counterclockwise until oil pressure reached 75 psi throughout the bearings and valvetrain. Afterward, the team cleaned and gapped the dual ignition points, installed fresh Autolite racing spark plugs gapped to 0.035 inches (0.89 mm), bolted on a new 650-cfm Holley four-barrel carburetor, and restored 12-volt power to the starter solenoid.
When the 351 Cleveland finally coughed to life from a temporary fuel jug, muffled exhaust notes and a shower of acorns revealed that squirrels had packed the mufflers solid over the decades. Angelo promptly sliced the exhaust pipes off behind the long-tube headers, allowing the V8 to idle smoothly (with 18 degrees of ignition advance) and fire all eight cylinders for the first time in more than three decades.
Despite the engine's crisp throttle response , the Mustang remains temporarily immobile inside the garage until its driveline and safety systems are rebuilt. Testing on the lift showed that the transmission had leaked its gear oil, the brake pedal was frozen, the radiator wept coolant, and the clutch assembly refused to engage, leaving Angelo with clear mechanical priorities before taking the revived Mach 1 onto public roads for its maiden drive in the third millennium.
Photo: YouTube/Stay Tuned Cars like Angelo's Philadelphia rescue come from a pivotal moment in Ford's golden-era muscle-car history. Introduced in August 1968 for the 1969 model year, the Mach 1 package transformed the Mustang Sportsroof fastback into an aggressive street machine equipped with competition suspension, matte-black hood paint, locking hood pins, deluxe interior trim, and potent V8 engines.
The Mach 1 was designed to bridge the gap between regular Mustang GTs and costly, limited-production Shelby variants. For 1970, Ford refined the body styling with cleaner single headlights and introduced the legendary 351-cubic-inch Cleveland V8, named after the Ohio foundry where it was cast.
Featuring thin-wall casting, canted valves, and massive cylinder-head ports, the four-barrel M-code Cleveland delivered 300 horsepower at 5,400 rpm with an 11:1 compression ratio as a $48 option, helping Ford sell 40,975 Mach 1 units out of 191,522 total Mustangs built that year.
Photo: YouTube/Stay Tuned The Mach 1 moniker itself originated a decade earlier during the height of Jet Age aerospace ambition, long before the Mustang existed. In a groundbreaking 1959 showcase, Ford stylist Gale Halderman, who later helped pen the original Mustang, co-designed the Ford Levacar Mach 1, a futuristic, wheel-less concept vehicle engineered to glide above specialized rails on a thin cushion of compressed air at speeds approaching the sound barrier (what science refers to as “Mach 1”).
Although the hovercar never reached production, Ford executives retained the evocative aerospace name, applying it to a chopped-roof Mustang concept car in 1967 and 1968 before launching the street-legal Mach 1 for 1969. That inaugural production run achieved instant commercial and motorsport credibility, moving 72,459 cars (some 25% of total Mustang production) in its first year.
Photo: YouTube/Stay Tuned It also set nearly 300 speed and endurance records on Utah's Bonneville Salt Flats and winning national manufacturer rally titles. Over subsequent generations, the Mach 1 nameplate adapted to shifting automotive eras, surviving the 1974 downsizing onto the Mustang II through 1978, returning in 2003 and 2004 with a shaker-hood 4.6-liter V8, and re-emerging from 2021 through 2023 as a 5.0-liter Coyote-powered track-focused coupe.
The 1970 M-code Mach 1 (351C V8 plus 4-speed) was quite rare back in the day, with only 2,937 examples assembled, according to Kevin Marti’s research. For reference, the 428 Cobra Jets came in at 2,501 (both manuals and automatics, though). This particular machine is not a run-of-the-mill ’70 Mustang Mach 1, but a personal challenge for the YouTubing wrencher-rescuer. Promising, but challenge nonetheless.

Rolls-Royce Ghost Shooting Brake Wants To Redefine the Luxury Family Car – Rendering
8 photos
Photo: Instagram | Kelsonik
Has Rolls-Royce expanded its lineup with a veritable family-oriented cruiser as a low-riding alternative to the Cullinan? After all, that’s what a five-door version of its Ghost luxury sedan would be.
The answer is obviously no. As we said in the title, this is a mere rendering of such a project, and before delving into some of the things that define it, we have to mention the obvious. And that’s the fact that something like this will never happen.
First and foremost, it would be a niche car, with no direct competitors. After all, it’s not like Mercedes-Maybach and Bentley want to add station wagon versions of their S-Class and Flying Spur, respectively. Second, estates are not exactly popular anymore, with crossovers and SUVs stealing their thunder, so Rolls-Royce will definitely not risk injecting a huge amount of money into something that might not sell in sufficient numbers to justify the investment.
With this information off our chest, let’s move on to the actual car itself, which was sketched out by @kelsonik and shared on his social media a few days ago. The rendered Rolls-Royce Ghost Shooting Brake features the same front fascia as the sedan. In fact, it is pretty much identical up to the B-pillars. Further back, it has a much longer roofline, as well as bigger rear three-quarter windows, and redesigned rear three-quarter panels.
Photo: Instagram | Kelsonik The magic happens at the end, where it features a tailgate that opens up into a huge cargo area, instead of a traditional trunk lid. The taillights are identical, and so is the rear bumper. The tailpipes carry over from the real thing, and so does pretty much everything else. We can see that the fuel filler cap is still positioned on the right rear three-quarter panel, and that this thing features a green paint finish, some black elements, and rides on entirely new wheels that are much larger than the standard ones.
Based on the facelifted iteration of the Rolls-Royce Ghost, namely the Series II, this virtual project also features the same interior, although it is not visible in these digital illustrations. This means the same three separate displays behind the full-width glass panel, as well as the Spirit operating system, choreographed interior illumination sequence, and almost countless personalization options and high-end features, among other things.
Power would also be supplied by the familiar V12 engine, which is a twin-turbocharged unit, in case you forgot. The mill has a 6.75-liter displacement, and develops 563 hp (571 ps/420 kW) and 627 pound-feet (850 Nm) of torque. The Rolls-Royce Ghost takes 4.6 seconds to reach 60 mph (97 kph) from a standstill, and 4.8 seconds from 0-62 mph (0-100 kph). As for its top speed, it is electronically limited to 155 mph (250 kph).
Those who want more goodies from their Rolls-Royce Ghost can get the superior Black Badge. It features a few updates inside and out, comes with 22-inch forged wheels, and offers more oomph. The output is now officially rated at 592 hp (600 ps/441 kW) and the peak thrust stands at 664 pound-feet (900 Nm). However, that does not make it faster, because the company quoted the same 4.6 seconds from 0-60 mph as in the regular version of the luxury sedan.
Photo: Instagram | Kelsonik Even though it competes against the likes of the Bentley Flying Spur and the Mercedes-Maybach S-Class, the Rolls-Royce Ghost is a lot more expensive than its main rivals in the class. For the 2027 model year, you are looking at a minimum of $375,000 for one of these, and it can easily exceed $425,000. Some versions of the car can cost half a million dollars. The Flying Spur starts from over $250,000, and the Maybach S-Class is available from more than $210,000.
Some say that the Ghost is the absolute best-of-the-best in its class, arguing that the S-Class and the Flying Spur do not come anywhere near it. Others would agree to disagree, and they’d pick the Mercedes-Maybach or the Bentley over the Rolls-Royce all day, any day. But if there is one Rolls-Royce that has no direct rivals, it is the Phantom. This gargantuan sedan sits in a league of its own, measuring up to 235.5 inches (5,981 mm) in length for the EWB (Extended Wheelbase), which has 184.5 inches (3,772 mm) between the axles.
As you likely recall, all vehicles currently made by Rolls-Royce utilize the same construction. The platform is called the Architecture of Luxury, and it is the foundation stone not only of the Ghost and Phantom luxury sedans, but also the Cullinan luxury SUV, and the Spectre luxury electric grand tourer. And no, no Bimmers are based on this platform.
Now, assuming that Rolls-Royce would indeed go ahead and green light the Ghost Shooting Brake , would you spend your money on a station wagon version of the British luxury sedan? That’s a tough question to answer, but for what it’s worth, I definitely like the design as sketched out by the quoted pixel master. Do you? EICMA 2026 • Here Are Some of the Serious and Obscure Brands That EICMA 2026 Had To Offer – Worth Knowing About
29 New Hot Wheels to Start Hunting for Soon
94 photos
Photo: Lamley Group
For most of the years I have collected Hot Wheels, I was quick to open any new package I got. Now, I have a line-up of nine cool Ferraris waiting in a box inside my car for several days. I guess this is what happens when you order too many 1/64th-scale models.
That’s not what I wanted to talk about today, though. Before I dive into the main topic though, let me just say that I had completely forgotten Mattel had started using Treasure Hunt collectibles in the Monster Truck series too. Will Trash It All arrived in Mix 2 this year, and uses the same black and gold paint scheme as the other three models: Duck N' Roll (Mix 5), Gotta Go (Mix 8) and Helichopper (Mix 12).
The latter the only one here that isn’t Brendon Vetuskey’s casting, and it won’t be the last time you’ll hear about its designer (Kurnia Alim). You’ll also notice some photos of a few interesting Hot Wheels storage solution, plus a hint about what seems to be an upcoming F1 chase car inside of an 8-Pack. I’ve got an even better F1 racer saved for the end of this story, and you might like to know that it will be available quite soon.
Anyway, let’s have a look at some of the 2027 previews available after the 40th Annual Hot Wheels Collectors Convention in Los Angeles. I’ll only refer to the cars I haven’t already discussed in previous stories, which means you’ll spot more than just 29 collectibles in the photo gallery. The first one that surprised me was the new variation of Fraser Campbell’s Porsche 908-3. This new livery takes after Claude Haldi’s car from the ‘70s, and is sadly missing the Toblerone and Shell decals.
Things are just like that in the Mainline series. Pass’n Go gets a new golden variation and it’s slightly better than the latest Drop Tops release. The 1965 Honda RA272 isn’t all that different this time around, and it’s safe to say that I’m glad we have a driver inside. The '69 Ford Mustang Boss 302 is still one of my all-time favorite Hot Wheels castings, even though it’s just half a decade away from its 20th anniversary.
A new Morgan is coming! Photo: Lamley Group It’s stunning in green, and I don’t even mind the black wheels for once. I’m not as excited about the latest variation of Corvette Grand Sport Roadster, and it’s not often that I’m completely uninterested in one of Brendon Vetuskey’s projects. We haven’t seen a Mainline version of the '73 BMW 3.0 CSL Race Car since 2022, as it has shown up as either a Premium or Silver Series collectibles over the past few years.
With this new livery, I’m certain it will fly off the pegs the moment it arrives in toy stores worldwide. As crazy as this might sound, I’d rather have the 2018 Bentley Continental GT3 instead: isn’t it amazing in grey and orange? The 2026 Morgan Super Sport comes as a huge surprise, as it’s only the second Morgan in Mattel’s portfolio. I wasn’t a fan of the Super 3, bu the Super Sport is playing in a different league.
The Aerodisc wheels are a bonus at this point, whereas the Armeria Lilac paint job will be the highlight here. The light blue Pontiac GTO is new to the game, but I’d be lying if I said I can accurately identify which casting this is. There are quite a few of them out there and I’m not a Pontiac specialist either. The yellow R34 GT-R will be one of the hottest cars in 2027, and I’m under the impression I’ve discussed about it before.
The next Treasure Hunt is a Tooned model Photo: Lamley Group It’s certainly in a league of its own, and not just because of those six-spoke wheels. Ryu Asada’s Nissan Skyline RS (KDR30) had two variations in 2026, and hasn’t had a Mainline release since 2024. It had the 3-spoke wheels when it was a Mystery Model in 2025, and I honestly regret not buying the Boulevard variation when I had the chance. While I enjoy bright colors on cars, I have mixed feelings about this light blue finish.
It will certainly be a peg-warmer next to the Stingassic Six Dodge, as that’s the kind of livery that might keep collectors enthusiastic for a few more years. The new Viper SRT almost feels like a page out of Neon Speeders, and it reminds me that we’re getting a special version of the iconic American machine in the Red Line Club next year. I almost fell out of my chair when I spotted the Tooned Purple Passion.
Not only is the color combo brilliant, but this is also a Regular Treasure Hunt for 2027! We don’t usually see previews of TH models until the day someone in Asia is able to do an unboxing for the world to see what’s coming up. The fifth iteration of Drift Ender is heading to a mini-series called Circuit Breakers, hence the unusual look. You’ll spot a few more quirky original castings in the photo gallery: they’re not something I want in my collection.
The Rondres W-33 is an exception for me: Ronald Wong and Andres Andrieu collaborated on this project. It’s styled after an early 2000s supercar, and it reminds me of either the Saleen S7 or the Jaguar XJ220 (which is obviously older than that). It’s the kind of project that makes me think fantasy castings aren’t so bad after all. I imagine kids won’t even mind that sort of thing. If you’re a fan of “Then and Now”, you’ll love the two, red, Honda Civics.
Forget about purple Lamborghinis, look at the Ferrari! Photo: Lamley Group
An FL5 would have been nicer than the FK8 but it’s still a Premium exclusive for now with no signs of joining the basic series anytime soon. After the two variations for Lil Mad, you’ll catch a glimpse of another Super Treasure Hunt for 2027 .
I don’t even want to imagine how much eBay seller will be asking for it in a few months from now. A Camaro 5-Pack wasn’t on my bingo card for next year: seeing just four of them in this previous is one way to create some excitement for the final version of the set.
It’s shaping up to be one of the best 5-Packs next year regardless of what other collectible Mattel is currently keeping secret. There’s certainly no shortage of options, especially with two new Camaro castings on their way.
Moving on to the Ferrari part of the story, the 12Cilindri comes as no surprise. And while the Ferrari 308 GTS looks decent enough in white, the purple Dino might almost start a treasure hunt if you ask me.
Disney and F1 together? Photo: Mattel Creations It immediately reminded me of the purple Ferrari F50 Challenge from 2001, which makes me want to go out to my car in the blistering cold to check if I have any purple Ferraris in my new package, too.
With all that behind us now, here’s another Hot Wheels surprise I didn’t see coming: the Disney x Formula 1 collab! I’m not saying I’m itching to get one for my collection, but I imagine the more hardcore F1 fans will like a closer look.
You’ll get three sets of Pirelli tires in the package, a new livery, and all for just $25. It might feel surprisingly cheap for a Mattel Creations Collaboratory special release, until you remember there are no opening parts like you’d typically get in the RLC series.
Oh well, it goes live on the manufacturer’s website on November 19 , 2026 at 9 AM PT. Your guess is as good as mine when thinking about how it might perform. It’s a case of love it or hate it, especially after what I’ve seen with last year’s first edition release of Fraser Campbell’s RLC-only casting.

Used Lamborghini Revuelto Hits the Used Car Market Stateside, What’s Your Take on the Price?
8 photos

Supercars come in numerous sizes and shapes these days, as the offer has never been so vast. Still, the majority of the petrolhead crowd has a favorite brand, and if yours is Lamborghini, then you have come to the right place, because we just encountered this Revuelto that is searching for a new home in the New World as we speak.
The model needs no introduction, especially if you have a soft spot for the Raging Bull’s modern-day machines. That’s because it is the company’s new-age flagship supercar, which replaced the Aventador some three years ago. The latter was preceded by the Murcielago, Diablo, Countach, and Miura in this order, and do you know what each and every one of these models has in common, besides the Lamborghini logo?
Well, they all feature a V12. And the automaker wasn’t willing to drop it for the modern-day Revuelto . That’s great news for the gearhead crowd, as not only does this model feature a great V12 mounted behind the passenger compartment, but it is a naturally aspirated unit, too, for faster responses. Nevertheless, it does feature electric assistance in order to meet the latest emission regulations, and it is a plug-in hybrid model in case you forgot.
The peak output is officially rated at 1,001 hp (747 kW/1,015 ps), and that’s more than the original Bugatti Veyron. The Revuelto takes only 2.5 seconds to sprint to 62 mph (100 kph), and pushes up to 217 mph (350 kph). The Revuelto SV, which is a significantly upgraded variant, has 1,050 hp (783 kW/1,065 ps) in total, is one-tenth of a second faster, and will reach 216 mph (348 kph). And that’s not a typo, because these numbers can be easily verified online.
Photo: Instagram | limitedspec Buying a brand new Lamborghini Revuelto means paying over $600,000 for the 2027 model year, and that’s definitely no bargain. The Revuelto SV is even more expensive, as it will set you back nearly $750,000. And that’s before the often-greedy dealer markups, as well as before checking any boxes on the options list. But how much is a used example?
Just because you are willing to buy used does not mean that you will pay pennies on the dollar. In fact, the market today shows that the Revuelto still tends to fetch over $600,000, and some copies can easily exceed $700,000, whereas others have just dropped below the $600K mark. A good machine requires blowing more than $600K, for what it’s worth. And this brings us to the supercar pictured in the gallery, which is for sale today in USA.
It is advertised by @limitedspec on social media, which reveals that the odometer reads 6,187 miles (9,957 km), and it is not considered a low-mileage example, because it is on the exotic side of things. Therefore, we can say that this car has seen plenty of action ever since it rolled off the line a few years ago. A low-mileage one has less than 1,000 miles (1,600 km) under its belt.
This Lamborghini Revuelto has a Bianco Monocerus paint finish beneath the wrap, which is matte black. The glossy black wheels, which spin around the red brake calipers, appear to be original, and on the inside, it offers a mix of white and black leather and Alcantara upholstery, with white piping and stitching, and the Lamborghini logo embroidered into the headrests.
Photo: Instagram | limitedspec It looks like the windows have been tinted, so the wrap is not the only mod, but for what it’s worth, this supercar definitely looks great. In fact, it is almost perfect, this writer would say, as the model rocks the stealth fighter jet-like look like a champ. The only thing needed to look perfect, in my opinion, would be a black Alcantara interior with a few red touches here and there for a bit of contrast.

After all, what’s the worse that they can say? No?

Rare 1958 Oldsmobile 88 Fiesta Wagon Flexes Even Rarer Engine Banned by NASCAR
15 photos
Photo: Mecum Auctions
In 1953, Oldsmobile used the Fiesta badge on a special-edition convertible based on the 98 model. It was part of a trio of drop-tops built by GM to promote its design leadership, and it was quite expensive. Four years later, Oldsmobile revived the name for a station wagon.
The latter arrived in 1957 and was based on the slightly shorter 88 model. Initially a hardtop-style wagon, the Fiesta was discontinued for good after the 1964 model year. It was replaced by the Vista Cruiser.
Station wagons aren't associated with high performance, but the Fiesta was briefly offered with a beefed-up V8. It happened toward the end of the 1950s, when Oldsmobile joined the Tri-Power craze with a six-barrel version of its iconic Rocket V8 engine. And it's tied to NASCAR racing.
In 1949, Oldsmobile had this crazy idea to bridge the gap between the 76 and 98 models with a car that would combine the smaller body of the former with the engine of the latter. The Rocket-powered 88 was born, and it immediately became a dominant force in stock car racing .
The 88 won races and championships through 1951, when it was eclipsed by the Hudson Hornet. Oldsmobile won its third and final manufacturers' title in 1955, but that's not to say it didn't try again. In 1957, the division created the J-2 package for this specific purpose.
The bundle replaced the four-barrel carburetor of the 371-cubic-inch (6.1-liter) Rocket V8 with a 3x2 setup and added a cast-iron intake manifold, forged pistons, a solid-lifter cam, and adjustable rocker arms. The compression ratio also increased from 9.5:1 to 10:1. The venture, however, was short-lived; NASCAR banned multiple carburetion (and fuel injection) a few months later.
The J-2 was also offered on the production 88. The streetable package did not include the forged pistons and solid-lifter cam, but the Tri-Power setup was enough to increase output by nearly 10%. The 88 J-2 hit showrooms with an impressive 300 horsepower and 415 pound-feet (563 Nm) of torque.
Although the engine was banned from racing, the option returned in 1958, this time around with more power (312 horsepower). However, it was discontinued later that year due to poor sales. It's unclear exactly how many J-2 cars were sold, but most experts agree that Olds built fewer than 2,500 examples. The 1958 Fiesta you see here is one of those cars.
And yes, the fact that it's a station wagon makes it that much rarer. Likely only 1% of all 88s sold in 1958 got the J-2 option, which puts the number of wagons fitted with this option into two-digit territory (Olds sold only 5,175 Fiestas). We're also looking at one of only 39 wagons known to exist, so it could very well be the only J-2 version out there.
Fortunately, this Fiesta did not end up in a junkyard like many of its siblings. The grocery-getter got a professional restoration, and it still has the 371 Rocket J-2 under the hood. It did get an electric fuel pump and aftermarket air cleaners, but it's pretty stock otherwise.
Previously parked in the St. Louis Car Museum, the 88 Fiesta is now looking for a home via Mecum Auctions. The wagon will go under the hammer at Kansas City 2026 on December 5. How much is this rare 88 worth?

EICMA 2026 • MTPeak Stole Some of the Spotlight at EICMA 2026 With Insane Power and Retro Looks on Three Wheels
Six Ghost Supercars That almost Reached Production Before Someone Pulled the Plug
42 photos
Photo: Jaguar
Traditionally speaking, most concept cars are understood by everyone to be fiction. Almost nobody who sees one for the first time expects them to ever reach a showroom, especially when it comes to flamboyant supercar concepts, and their makers don’t expect it either.
That is not exactly the case with the following vehicles, because all of them had engineering teams, and most of them even had running prototypes or even announced production numbers. In some cases, they even had expected pricing or a list of customers ready to open their wallets for a production version.
Sadly, at one point late in the process, usually someone in charge of the budget decided to abruptly end the entire program. That is how all of the following “ghost” supercars ended up in the history books. They existed physically, some even as running prototypes, but only got featured in magazines, video games or even movies, but not in the hands of actual people who would have bought them.
The Jaguar C-X75 is the most recent such case, as a little over a year after being unveiled as a concept car at the 2010 Paris Motor show, Jaguar announced that it would build 250 examples with Williams Advanced Engineering. The production version was to use an entirely different powertrain but equally as radical as the concept, and it seems that about 100 potential customers expressed interest in buying the million-dollar hybrid supercar.
Fast forward to December 2012, and Jaguar cancelled the production because of the global economic climate, albeit it had already built five working prototypes. The shell of a C-X75, this time powered by a supercharged V8, made a surprising cameo appearance a few years later in the James Bond film Spectre, where the villain played by Dave Bautista chased Bond through Rome in one of seven actual stunt cars that Jaguar and Williams had built for the movie.
You could say that a similar story happened with the Chrysler ME Four-Twelve, which was a near-production supercar concept built around a quad-turbocharged AMG V12 with 850 horsepower. That project also ended up in the bid after Chrysler backed away for cost reasons.
A lot closer to production was the first-generation Audi R8 with a twin-turbocharged V12 diesel to complement the gasoline V8 and V10, with Ferdinand Piech adamant that such a monstrosity would do wonders for the brand’s image. It too saw working prototypes built, albeit the arrival of the global financial crisis quickly made the investment implausible.
There are only a few supercar concepts that followed a similar timeline in recent decades, and what brings them together is how close each one was to actually going into production. Neither of them got the chance to truly amaze or disappoint anyone, so nobody knows how they would have been received by real customers.
The only remaining physical memory from some of them, apart from the actual concepts or prototypes that managed to be built, are the technology patents or maybe even the powertrains they previewed. They each have an important place in the automotive history books though, and they should be celebrated as “what could have been.”
Mercedes-Benz C112: Over 700 Orders For a Phantom Supercar Most cancelled supercars on this list didn’t end up in production for fear that they wouldn’t sell and/or various global economic reasons, but that is not the case with the innovative Mercedes-Benz C112 concept, unveiled to great success at the 1991 Frankfurt Motor Show. Unlike the other examples, the C112 actually received no less than 700 orders, and Mercedes-Benz still declined to build it.
The concept car was born out of Stuttgart’s incredibly successful return to sports car racing, after the Sauber-Mercedes partnership won them the Group C world championship and even the 24 Hours of Le Mans race. In fact, pretty much everyone thought that the C112 was built to celebrate that success and as a road-going counterpart to the Mercedes C11 that won the 1990 Group C championship..
Photo: Mercedes-Benz AG As an ode to the legendary 300 SL, the mid-engine supercar used upward-opening doors and, despite being styled by Bruno Sacco’s design team at Mercedes-Benz, the concept car was actually built by Carrozzeria Coggiola, in Turin. Probably following this success, Mercedes would collaborate with Coggiola on other outlandish concept cars from the 1990s and early 2000s as well.
The engine powering the C112 was the then-new 6.0-liter V12 from the S-Class, which delivered a healthy 408 PS (402 HP) and 580 Nm (428 lb-ft). Codenamed M120, versions of it would go on to power the Pagani Zonda as well, but the C112 was the first car in which it was ever paired with a six-speed manual transmission.
What surrounded that engine was a lot more impressive, and I’m not even talking about the design. In fact, the C112 was the first Mercedes-Benz to feature a version of the Active Body Control suspension system, which was still circa 8 years away from debuting in production in the CL-Class of 1999. It also had electronically controlled rear-wheel-steering, tire pressure monitoring and an early version of radar-guided cruise control.
On top of it, it also had active aerodynamics, with the front spoiler and massive but usually hidden rear wing adjusting themselves depending on speed. The rear wing could also flip up to act as an airbrake, a concept that harked back to versions of the 1950s 300 SLR, and that would only debut in production on the SLR McLaren over a decade later.
While the 4.9 seconds required to go from 0 to 100 kph (62 mph) and the 309 kph (192 mph) top speed were not exactly ground-breaking, the 998 kg (2,200 lb) of downforce at top speed was. No less than 700 people placed orders in blind for the C112 following its reveal, but Mercedes executives decided that the brand didn’t need a flagship supercar and that its success in motorsport was enough marketing.
Ford GT90: A Quad-Turbocharged V12 Ford That Never Got to Be When the GT90 appeared at Ford’s booth at the 1995 Detroit Auto Show, everyone thought it would be Detroit’s answer to the McLaren F1. Despite its name drawing a connection to the Le Mans and Ferrari-destroying GT40, its design looked like something from a Sci Fi movie, especially in that white paint, featuring a triangular exhaust outlet.
Believe it or not, the Ford GT90 had been built in secrecy by a small team in a little over 6 months, at a reported cost of about $3 million. Because at the time Jaguar was owned by Ford, engineers borrowed heavily from the XJ220, with the GT90 sitting on a lengthened version of the Jaguar’s aluminum honeycomb chassis. It also used the model’s double-wishbone suspension and five-speed manual gearbox.
Photo: Ford What it didn’t use was a Jaguar engine, despite the British company having a V12 of its own, the GT90’s powertrain was actually a one-off, with the 5.9-liter, 48-valve V12 being based on Ford’s Modular V8. With the addition of four extra cylinders and four Garrett turbochargers, power was quoted at 730 PS (720 HP) and 895 Nm (660 lb-ft) of torque.
While it was never tested, Ford argued that that power was enough for the GT90 to hit 60 mph (97 kph) in just 3,1 seconds and reach an estimated top speed of 407 kph (253 mph), or enough to beat the McLaren F1 record at the time. Its exhaust allegedly would melt the surrounding bodywork, which is why the triangular outlet was accompanied by ceramic heat shielding.
Whether as a successor to the GT40 or as a stand-alone, world-beating supercar, everyone thought that the Ford GT90 was heading into production. Sadly, Ford didn’t budge at the massive interest surrounding the model, and the car remained a one-off tour de force. It did make the rounds on every major car racing video game of the late 1990s, and it’s probably the only American car of that era to print more bedroom posters than the Viper.
Chrysler ME Four-Twelve: A Running Prototype, Not a Concept Car The early 2000s were filled with a plethora of outlandish-looking concept cars from American carmakers, and the Chrysler ME Four-Twelve made no exception. However, unlike most of the others, the unconventional-looking (for a Chrysler) supercar was a running prototype, not just a rolling concept.
Its odd name was actually a description of its specifications, with the “ME” coming from “mid-engine,” “four” was the number of turbochargers, and “twelve” was the number of cylinders. Chrysler was part of the ill-fated DaimlerChrysler conglomerate at the time, so the engine was actually developed by AMG. Oddly enough, it wasn’t a modified version of the three-valves-per-cylinder M275 from the “65 AMG” models.
Photo: Chrysler Instead, the ME Four-Twelve resurrected the M120 6.0-liter that was also used in the C112, with four-turbochargers being attached to it thanks to the work of AMG and Pagani engineers. Output was a massive 862 PS (850 HP) and a gargantuan 1,152 Nm (850 lb-ft) of torque.
The rest of the car was equally serious, with the passenger cell being a mix of carbon fiber and aluminum honeycomb, while the gearbox of a transaxle, seven-speed dual-clutch made by Ricardo. The entire car weighed only 1,310 kg (2,888 pounds), meaning that the quoted 0 to 60 mph (97 kph) was a very much believable 2.9 seconds, while its top speed was estimated at 400 kph (248 mph).
Apart from the running concept car, Chrysler made another prototype, which it let loose on Laguna Seca at the hands of journalists, but with a detuned version of the engine. At the time, people were expecting it to enter production in 2006, but something along the way went wrong. Allegedly, Mercedes didn’t like that Chrysler would have a more powerful supercar than their own SLR McLaren, but the most probable motive was that Chrysler simply didn’t want to invest hundreds of millions in such a project without the reassurance that it would also make money.
Acura Advanced Sports Car Concept: The Lexus LFA Rival That Never Was Not long after the original NSX went out of production in 2005, Honda and Acura made no secret of wanting to replace it, and the first hint of a successor appeared at the 2007 Detroit Auto Show. Unlike its RWD, V6-powered, mid-engine predecessor, the Acura Advanced Sports Car Concept was a front-engined coupe with a naturally aspirated V10 with all-wheel-drive.
In short, it turned the original formula around, and people didn’t seem to mind it. That said, the show car itself was a non-running model, with the technical details actually coming from Honda executives after it was unveiled. They confirmed the V10 and SH-AWD system, with report putting the powertrain’s displacement at around 5.0-liter, while its output was expected to be in the 500 to 600 HP ballpark.
Photo: Acura In short, Honda was working on a direct rival to both the Nissan GT-R R35 and the Lexus LFA. Initially, the ASCC’s design received a lukewarm response, so Honda apparently sent it back to the drawing board several times before announcing that the NSX’s replacement would be launched sometime in 2010.
For over a year, engineering was in full throttle, with several camouflaged prototypes being tested at the Nurburgring Nordschleife, where the new NSX was supposed to beat the Nissan GT-R’s time. Unfortunately, the 2008 world financial crisis reached Japan as well, and Honda was forced to announce that the V10-powered NSX successor would halt development, coinciding with the carmaker’s exit from Formula 1 as well.
Those camouflaged prototypes did get an unusual afterlife though, with the HSV-010 GT competing in Japan’s super GT series between 2010 and 2013 using them as base, despite the road car having been canceled. It remains one of the very few racing cars derived from a production model that was never produced.
Audi R8 V12 TDI: The Diesel Supercar That Would Have Changed Everything Oddly enough, a diesel-powered supercar seemed like a reasonable idea back in 2008, especially for Audi, which had won the 24 Hours of Le Mans in both 2006 and 2007 using the devil’s fuel. On top of it, back then diesel was the king of European car sales, so putting the two together looked like the obvious step for the Ingolstadt carmaker.
As one of Ferdinand Piech’s babies, as he was the one who pushed the most for its existence, the Audi R8 V12 TDI was unveiled at the 2008 Detroit Auto Show. Instead of the gasoline V8 or V10 from the regular R8, behind the seats sat a 6.0-liter, twin-turbocharged V12 diesel, which delivered 500 PS (493 HP) and a massive 1,000 nm (738 lb-ft) of torque.
Photo: Audi AG Even crazier was that all that oomph was delivered to all four wheels through a six-speed manual transmission instead of a double-clutch or an automatic. Audi quoted 4.2 seconds to 100 kph (62 mph) and a top speed of more than 300 kph (186 mph), making the diesel just a tad quicker than the V8-powered, gasoline version.
That said, the car had a lot of issues with packaging, as the V12 diesel was not only much larger than the V8, but also made the car about 300 kg (661 pounds) heavier. It also needed far more cooling, so the vents grew by some 20 percent, and a NACA duct was cut into the roof to feed air to the intercoolers.
Even the suspension and brakes were reworked to handle the extra weight, and all these changes were definitely quite manageable on what was essentially a show car. What was not manageable was lifting all those modifications to series production standards, which is why Audi announced that the cost of re-engineering the R8 around such a massive engine was simply too great for recouping the investment from sales, especially since the financial crisis was in full swing at the time.
Jaguar C-X75: The One That Almost Made It Surprisingly, no car on this list got further than the Jaguar C-X75 on the way to production. The British carmaker even put a price on it and hired a Formula 1 team to engineer it, going as far as even building five working prototypes before cancelling it.
The original concept appeared at the 2010 Paris Motor Show, and, as its name suggested, it was built to mark Jaguar’s 75th anniversary. What was unusual about it was its choice of powertrain, with the model being powered by four YASA electric motors before they were cool, with two small gas turbines acting as generators.
Photo: Jaguar A year later, it was confirmed to go into production, with Jaguar planning to build 250 of them in collaboration with Williams Advanced Engineering, and start of sales was set for 2013. The Range-extending electric powertrain from the concept was replaced with an equally innovative powertrain.
This time, the production version was supposed to be powered by a 1.6-liter four-cylinder that was both supercharged and turbocharged, and which could rev to 10,000 rpm. The engine delivered 509 PS (502 HP) on its own, but was augmented by two more YASA electric motors for a combined output of 862 PS (850 HP) and 1,000 Nm (738 lb-ft) of torque. The prototypes apparently reached 322 kph (200 mph) in testing, with a theoretical maximum speed of 354 kph (220 mph).
When all was said and done, around 100 potential customers expressed interest in buying one, and this was likely not enough to persuade Jaguar executives to forget how much it tried to sell every unit of the unsuccessful XJ220. At the end of 2012, the carmaker announced that the global economic climate wasn’t exactly friendly to launching a million dollar supercar, so the project was canceled.

Woman Walks Into a Dealership, Wants To Trade in Her Ram 1500 TRX for an Audi R8
15 photos
Photo: Toronto Auto Brokers | YouTube
A woman brought in her Ram 1500 TRX, hoping to drive home in an Audi R8. She drives a hard bargain, trying to get as much money as possible for the pickup truck. She loves it, but she realized she doesn’t really need it. Besides, it gives her back pain. Instead, she hopes to go home in something very different from the super truck: a first-generation Audi R8 with the very much sought-after gated manual.
The woman is not just any customer. She is Trina, the one who used to work for the luxury dealership in Toronto, Canada. She used to make the videos that promoted the cars listed for sale by the dealership. She did the walkarounds, proving she was a real car enthusiast who obviously knew her way around cars.
Trina had a Ford F-150 Raptor before the TRX and calls the upgrade " wicked ." She bought the TRX with 80,000 kilometers (48,710 miles) on the clock from a chicken farmer. Now it is parked in the dealership yard with 91,155 kilometers (56,641 miles). She may not have driven it much, but she put it through its paces while moving: she transported sod in the cargo bed. " It's not like a garage princess ," she says.
The " not a princess " truck is a Level 2, which brings the leather and suede upholstery, the leather and suede-wrapped steering wheel, a head-up display and contrasting stitching, along with heated and cooled front and back seats and the 19-speaker Harman Kardon sound system.
Photo: Toronto Auto Brokers | YouTube She has dogs, but they didn’t like the truck's typical high ride. They probably hated the brisk accelerations as well. The 2021 Ram 1500 TRX rolled off the production line with the 6.2-liter supercharged HEMI V8, pumping out 702 horsepower (712 metric horsepower) and 650 pound-feet (881 Newton meters) of torque. That is enough for a run from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 4.5 seconds and a top speed of 118 mph (190 kph).
Those dogs surely won't like what she’s getting. She plans to trade in the TRX for a 2012 Audi R8 with a gated manual. The first-generation R8 that Trina wants is set in motion by the 5.2-liter V10 with naturally aspirated firepower. The V10 pushes out 518 horsepower (525 metric horsepower) and 391 pound-feet (530 Newton meters) of torque.
That makes it flash from 0 to 60 in 3.7 seconds on its way to a top speed of 196 mph (316 kph). A six-speed gated manual puts the power down through all four corners, which translates to fun behind the wheel. Back then, Audi also offered the six-speed automated manual, the R-tronic, while the range-topping R8 GT came exclusively with the R-tronic.
The Audi R8 is going to be a toy for Trina and her fiancé. They actually have a garage full of motorized toys. They have a Porsche 911 GT3 RS and have recently purchased a BMW M3 Competition G80 . Trina has been dailying the TRX, but the M3 is going to become her daily once she sells the truck. She also has an 11-year-old Lexus IS, but she keeps that one as an ambition: she swore she would take it to 500,000 miles, and she's halfway there.
Photo: Toronto Auto Brokers | YouTube The dealer, Gideon, offers her $77,000 CAD ($49,051 US), but she doesn’t even want to hear about any price under $80,000 CAD ($56,058). She paid $90,000 CAD ($63,065 US) back in January for the TRX and won’t let go of it without a fight. Besides, she bought a $5,000 warranty for the truck.
She is well aware that the TRX is slowly depreciating and sees the swap as a smart financial investment. Across the entire 2006–2015 generation, Audi built roughly 28,000 R8s in total, and only a small fraction combined the 5.2-liter V10 with the gated manual gearbox. So Trina expects the Audi R8 ’s value to grow over the years.
She is also getting rid of the 2021 Ram 1500 TRX because of the hard seats. Now she is still suffering from back pain caused by a car accident and is driving with a cushion that she sits on. She hopes to feel better in the bucket seats of the R8.
In Canada, a 2012 Audi R8 5.2 V10 with the six-speed gated manual typically sells for $155,000 to $200,000+ CAD, depending on mileage and condition. That translates to approximately $108,640 to $140,180 USD.
Photo: Toronto Auto Brokers | YouTube The dealer and the customer eventually strike a deal at $81,000 CAD ($56,745 USD) for the TRX. Gideon has already launched it at auction three times, and the most generous offer wasn’t anywhere near what he paid for the truck. The good news is that he sold a sports car in winter.
A couple of days later, Trina comes to pick up her new-to-her 2012 gated R8. " I think I paid too much for this car, " Gideon says when she drives off. Well, Trina sure is happy.

EICMA 2026 • Here Are Some of the Serious and Obscure Brands That EICMA 2026 Had To Offer – Worth Knowing About
1970 Plymouth Road Runner Packs the Holy Trinity: 426 Hemi, 4-Speed, for Sale, and It's a Lot
20 photos
Photo: REV! Muscle Cars
When Plymouth introduced the Road Runner for the 1968 model year, the mission was simple: strip away luxury fluff, drop in big-block Mopar muscle, and undercut every rival on price. Over half a century later, top-tier examples command serious collector money, and this 1970 Plymouth Road Runner 426 Hemi 4-speed hardtop proves why.
Documented with its original fender tag, factory broadcast sheets, and numbers-matching drivetrain, it represents classic Chrysler street warfare at its sharpest.
Plymouth built the Road Runner across 13 model years from 1968 through 1980, spanning three distinct B-body generations before transitioning to a compact trim package. The first generation ran from 1968 to 1970 on a 116-inch wheelbase, earning Motor Trend Car of the Year honors in 1969. A fuselage-styled second generation followed from 1971 to 1974 on a 115-inch platform, preceding a one-year 1975 B-body third generation and the 1976–1980 Plymouth Volaré era.
Body styles evolved dramatically as safety rules, insurance surcharges, and buyer tastes reshaped Detroit during the 1970s. Early buyers between 1968 and 1970 could order a two-door pillared coupe, a two-door hardtop, or—for 1969 and 1970 only—a two-door convertible, alongside the aerodynamic (but questionably looking) 1970 Superbird hardtop.
Photo: REV! Muscle Cars From 1971 through 1974, Plymouth restricted the Road Runner strictly to a two-door hardtop, before offering a two-door pillared coupe in 1975 and compact Volaré coupes afterward.
Engine choices defined the bird's reputation throughout its run. First-generation cars came standard with a 335-hp/425-lb-ft 383-cubic-inch four-barrel V8, while buyers could step up to the 390-hp 440 Six-Barrel or the 425-hp 426-cubic-inch Hemi. Subsequent generations introduced the 340, 400, 318, and 360 V8s—and even a 225-cubic-inch Slant-Six in 1979—mated across various years to 3-speed manual, 4-speed manual, 4-speed overdrive, or 3-speed TorqueFlite automatic transmissions.
By 1970, insurance premiums, and competition from Plymouth's own Duster and the restyled E-body Barracuda trimmed standard Road Runner production to 41,484 units worldwide (36,861 U.S. deliveries), plus at least 1,935 Superbirds. Hardtops led the tally at 24,944 cars, followed by 15,716 pillared coupes and 824 convertibles. Under the hood, 39,517 left the factory with the 383 V8, 1,815 carried the 440 Six-Barrel (introduced mid-year), and just 152 packed the 426 Hemi.
Photo: REV! Muscle Cars Within that 152-car Hemi run, Plymouth assembled 74 coupes, 3 convertibles, and 75 hardtops, splitting the hardtops into 59 examples with 4-speed manuals and 16 TorqueFlite automatics. While 1970 buyers could choose a 3-speed manual, 4-speed manual, or 3-speed automatic behind lesser engines, checking the E74 Hemi box added $871.45 to a $3,034 hardtop base price. Equipped with the A33 Track Pak and N96 Air Grabber, a hemi Road Runner could easily top $4,550.
For 1970, the Road Runner Hemi had lost a lot of its original touch. Back in ’68, when the moniker made landfall, nearly half of the 2,289 Hemi engines were dropped in a Road Runner (1,019 units). Just two years later, the percentage had fallen to about one in ten (152 out of a grand total of 1,543 Plymouths and Dodges armed with the mighty 426-cuber).
That original investment explains why surviving 4-speed Hemi hardtops sit near the top of the Mopar hierarchy. This St. Louis-built example left the line on January 20, 1970, and stayed with one family for over 30 years. It was restored once in their care, then it later received a thorough mechanical and cosmetic refresh before entering a private collection, showing 59,195 miles today.
Photo: REV! Muscle Cars Finished in factory EB5 Blue Fire Metallic across both its lower body and slick-top roof, the muscle car wears a purposeful sleeper specification. Whoever checked the order sheet skipped the optional hood blackout and fuselage dust trails, leaving only a white V8W transverse tail stripe, Road Runner fender decals, and subtle “Hemi” cowl badges to hint at its firepower. Quad headlights, a waterfall grille, J45 hood pins, and the N96 Air Grabber scoop complete the mugshot of this big-bore leviathan.
Inside, the cabin pairs Black Velvet upper door frames with charcoal-and-black premium vinyl bucket seats in crisp, blemish-free condition . A woodgrain center console frames the unmistakable Hurst pistol-grip shifter connected to the 4-speed cogbox. Full factory gauges include the Tic-Toc-Tach, complemented by an Music Master 2-watt AM radio and a woodgrain steering wheel with its working Road Runner horn button.
Beneath the Air Grabber hood sits the original 426 Hemi V8, breathing through dual Carter 4-barrel carburetors for 425 hp and 490 lb-ft of torque. Mopar authority Frank Badalson verified both the oil-pan rail VIN stamp and final assembly stamp as factory-authentic. OE Gold Award winner Steve Bean pulled and rebuilt the engine, K-member, and front suspension to concours standards, coating the block in Hemi Orange while preserving original pan casting runs.
Photo: REV! Muscle Cars Factory Track Pak hardware makes this hardtop far more than a straight-line showpiece. The package bundled a 9¾-inch Dana 60 rear axle with 3.54:1 Sure-Grip gears, Hemi-spec suspension, a 7-blade fan, and a 26-inch radiator, backed by B51 power front disc brakes. Underneath, rust-free frame rails and floor pans retain factory undercoating alongside rebuilt steering linkage, refinished torsion bars, resurfaced original rotors, balanced driveshaft, fresh shocks, and correct exhaust.
Serious Mopar collectors prize provenance almost as much as cubic inches, and this Road Runner backs up its hardware with an airtight paper trail. The original fender tag—complete with its matching 181 plant inspection stamp—and factory broadcast sheets reside in a document safe, accompanied by inspection reports and stamp photography.
Between its 1-of-59 drivetrain combination, long-term single-family history, and concours-fresh mechanicals, very few 1970 B-bodies check as many boxes. For enthusiasts hunting an investment-grade 4-speed Hemi Mopar with verified numbers and documented history, the wait might be over.
This 1970 Plymouth Road Runner is currently offered for sale by Rev Muscle Cars in Lake Villa, Illinois, carrying an asking price of $295,000. That puts it squarely in blue-chip collector territory, yet right in line with what top-flight, concours-detailed 1970 Hemi 4-speed hardtops command on today's market.
